newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German powerhouse lacks lustre at vital EMU stage.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German powerhouse lacks lustre at vital EMU stage.

text.p: Europe's powerhouse economy looked low on fuel on Wednesday.
German joblessness is at a post-war record, the budget deficit is too high and increased political pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl is posing a threat to the European Union's currency union plans.
In financial markets, German bonds were robust as traders rejoiced in concluding there was little chance for an official interest rate rise any time soon.

And the mark, which lost around seven percent against the dollar in January, took a new knock on speculation that Germany wanted a weaker currency to boost its export trade, prompting the Bundesbank to step in to give verbal support to the mark.

Kohl, who has faced a barrage of criticism since figures last wekk showed Germany's jobless soared to a record 4.66 million in January, stoutly defended his policies. He also angrily dismissed speculation by the news weekly Der Spiegel that he had cancer.
"I have experienced a lot of underhandedness in my political life but this is particularly shabby," Kohl, 66, told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.
It was Kohl's most robust riposte yet to a wave of speculation that he has no answers to soaring unemployment and an apparent lack of direction in his centre-right coalition.
Kohl also touched a raw nerve with unions angry at the record unemployment when he said Germans should accept little or no real pay gains in coming years in a bid to create jobs.
"Profits and share prices keep rising, exports hum along and unemployment also just keeps on rising," IG Metall leader Klaus Zwickel said in response.
"I think this proposal shows the Kohl government is pretty desperate for solutions," commented Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt.

With the record jobless figure expected to place an additional strain on the budget, a survey released on Wednesday showed that Germany -- once the model pupil in the EMU school -- could face problems qualifying legitimately for the euro.

A survey of 32 economists conducted by Reuters showed that five of the six countries expected to form the launch pad for a single currency were well on their way to meeting the required criteria for entry, but that Germany may lag behind.

Germany is seen overshooting slightly on the requirement that its 1997 budget deficit fall to three percent of gross domestic product and its debt to 60 percent, with a predicted deficit ratio of 3.05 percent and debt-to-GDP of 62 percent.
The economists said Germany was likely to gain a political entry ticket to EMU even if it missed the strict EMU goals, but warned that this could mean a credibility loss for the euro.

Wary that protracted mark weakness in the next few months could also hurt the euro's stability, the Bundesbank and Bonn finance ministry issued a two-pronged attack on a surging dollar, countering a report Germany wanted a stronger dollar.

Chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, in an official statement from the powerful central bank, said the Bundesbank continued to support a statement made by the Group of Seven industrial nations at a meeting in Berlin this weekend.
"That statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks (98 cents)," he said.
"We have nothing to add to the G7 statement," a finance ministry spokesman said.

On domestic issues, there was a hint of compromise on a planned tax reform when Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under pressure to win support of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), showed some flexibility on timing for the changes.

Against the backdrop of shrill SPD attacks on his fiscal policies, Waigel said the income tax reform could be brought forward to next year, instead of 1999, by making moderate cuts to both the entry level and top income tax rates.

The government coalition, made up of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union and the Free Democrats (FDP), has proposed a 30 billion mark net tax cut in 1999 that would cut the top rate to 39 percent.

The SPD, which can block parts of the tax reform with its majority in the upper house of parliament, has urged Bonn to bring forward the tax cuts to 1998. It opposes government plans to partly finance the reform by raising value added taxes. ($ = 1.682 German Marks)
